content: Self-reference is a phenomenon observed in both natural and formal languages, where a sentence or formula refers to itself either directly, through an intermediary, or via some form of encoding. In philosophy, self-reference pertains to the capacity of a subject to refer to themselves, as exemplified by the use of the pronoun I in English. This concept becomes feasible when there are two distinct logical levels: a primary level and a meta-level. Self-reference is frequently encountered in disciplines such as mathematics, philosophy, computer programming, and linguistics. However, self-referential statements can sometimes lead to paradoxes, though the significance of these paradoxes may be limited by the concept of antinomy. An example of self-reference can be found in the concept of autopoiesis, where a system's logical organization generates the physical structures that, in turn, recreate the system itself. In metaphysics, self-reference is associated with subjectivity, while its counterpart, hetero-reference (a term introduced by Niklas Luhmann), is linked to objectivity. In literature, self-reference occurs when an author refers to their own work within the context of that work. Notable examples include Cervantes's Don Quixote, Denis Diderot's Jacques the Fatalist and His Master, Italo Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveler, Nikolai Gogol's various stories, John Barth's Lost in the Funhouse, and Luigi Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author. This literary device is closely related to the concept of breaking the fourth wall or meta-reference, which often involves self-referential elements. The surrealist painter René Magritte is also renowned for his self-referential works, such as The Treachery of Images. In this painting, the phrase This is not a pipe challenges the viewer to consider whether this refers to the depicted pipe, the painting itself, or the sentence. Self-reference is also utilized in tautologies and in specific terminologies. For instance, when a word defines itself, such as Machine: any objects put together mechanically, the result is a tautology. These self-references can range from simple words to complex propositions, often requiring acceptance of the statement as self-evident or self-proving. In computer science, self-reference is exemplified by recursion, where a program or function relies on instances of itself to perform computations. The Lisp programming language is particularly designed to leverage recursion. Object-oriented programming languages also incorporate self-reference through special keywords that refer to the current instance of an object, such as this in C++, Java, and PHP; self in Smalltalk and Objective-C; and Me in Visual Basic. Examples of Self-Reference Mathematics Tupper's self-referential formula is a mathematical example of self-reference. Sentences This statement is short. I am not the subject of this sentence. 'I' is the subject of this sentence. Which question is also its own answer? The statement 'Yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation' yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation is an example of the liar paradox, involving indirect self-reference through a quine, which results in a paradox. The statement that the word 'false' should be interpreted as 'not true' is false is another version of the liar paradox. Russell's paradox involves the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, leading to a logical contradiction. The Examples section of this article refers to itself. This sentence exemplifies cacozelia (using rare or foreign words to appear learned). Do not read this. This page intentionally left blank. The Fumblerules Fumblerules are statements that illustrate rules of grammar or writing by violating those very rules. George L. Trigg and William Safire have compiled lists of such rules, but anyone with sufficient knowledge of grammar can create their own. For a more comprehensive list, refer to the List of Fumblerules. Literature Ishmael Reed's poem beware: do not read this poem is self-referential, as it warns against reading itself. The Monster at the End of This Book references itself in both its title and throughout the story. Abbie Hoffman's Steal This Book is self-referential in its title. Robert A. Heinlein's The Cat Who Walks Through Walls explores the concept of the universe (or multiverse) as an object manipulated by an author, including the plot of the book itself. Jostein Gaarder's Sophie's World features a protagonist who becomes aware that she is a character in a book. Michael Ende's The Neverending Story prominently employs self-reference, particularly when a character within the story (Atreyu) discovers a book titled The Neverending Story, which is the same book the reader is holding. Other Examples Self-enumerating pangrams are examples of self-reference in linguistics. A Wikipedia article titled Self-Reference is inherently self-referential. Article 52 of the Irish Constitution, despite being legally binding, has been prohibited from publication in official texts since 1938, creating a self-referential legal situation.
